passage: At the stationery shop near their Delhi colony, Madhuri, ten, held a glitter pen set: twelve pens, 350 rupees. In her pocket were the 400 rupees she had saved over four months from birthday money and small jobs for her mother. Her friend Farhan said, "Buy it! It's so shiny." Madhuri turned the box over. "I already have pens that work. And this is almost everything I saved." She put it back and bought one blue gel pen for twenty. Walking home, she felt a small sting when Farhan showed off his new eraser, then touched the notes still folded in her pocket.

qa.q: How much did the glitter pen set cost?
qa.a: 350 rupees.

qa.q: What did Madhuri feel walking home?
qa.a: A small sting of missing out, mixed with satisfaction as she touched the savings still in her pocket.

qa.q: What thinking helped Madhuri decide?
qa.a: She compared the price with how long it took to save and asked whether she really needed more pens.

qa.q: How might Farhan see Madhuri's choice?
qa.a: He may find it dull, since he was excited by the shiny set and wasn't thinking about the months of saving.

grounding: It shows a girl weighing a purchase against months of saving and choosing not to spend on something she doesn't need.

passage:
"Mumma, my bag strap tore. Can we buy a new one? Everyone has the new cartoon ones."
Gurleen turned the bag over in her hands. "The bag is fine. Only the strap. How much is a new bag?"
"Six hundred, I think."
"And what does the tailor charge to fix a strap?"
Gopika thought. "Maybe thirty?"
"So what's left from six hundred?"
"Five hundred seventy." She frowned. "That's a lot."
"We could use some of it for your school trip."
Gopika looked at the old bag. "Can the tailor put a patch? A star patch?"
"I'll ask."
"Then it'll be a new-ish bag."

qa.q: How much did Gopika think a new bag cost?
qa.a: Six hundred.

qa.q: Why did Gopika frown at "Five hundred seventy"?
qa.a: She was surprised and uneasy at how much would be spent replacing a whole bag when only the strap was broken.

qa.q: Why did Gurleen ask questions instead of just saying no?
qa.a: Working out the numbers let Gopika see the value of repairing herself, so the choice felt like hers.

qa.q: How might Gurleen feel about Gopika's star-patch idea?
qa.a: Pleased that Gopika chose repair over a new bag and made it her own, and happy to ask the tailor about the patch. 😊

grounding: It shows a girl working out the value of repairing rather than replacing and choosing the thrifty option.

passage: Last summer, when our town had water cuts, I learned what a bucket is worth. Rajni Aunty, who lives downstairs, said, "Come, Anjali, see," and showed me how she saved every drop: rice-washing water went to the tulsi, bath water mopped the stairs. At first I thought it was silly. Then one day the tanker didn't come, and our tank ran dry. Rajni Aunty's family still had water, because they'd used theirs three times over. Now I turn off the tap while brushing and collect the AC drip in a bucket. It feels small. But I remember that dry tank.

qa.q: Where did Rajni Aunty's rice-washing water go?
qa.a: To the tulsi.

qa.q: Why did Anjali first think Rajni Aunty's habits were silly?
qa.a: Anjali hadn't yet felt what running out was like, so saving every drop seemed unnecessary.

qa.q: What small habits did Anjali adopt?
qa.a: Turning off the tap while brushing and collecting the AC drip in a bucket.

qa.q: How might Rajni Aunty feel seeing Anjali copy her habits?
qa.a: Pleased that her example helped a young neighbour understand how precious water is.

grounding: It shows a child learning to respect a limited resource and avoid waste after seeing a neighbour's careful use.

passage: Class 4B shop day, teacher's note. Each child had twenty paper tokens to spend at the classroom stalls. Thomas walked the whole room before buying anything. He asked Rafiq, who ran the pencil stall, why an eraser cost three tokens and a sharpener five. Rafiq explained that the sharpener 'has a blade, so it's more work to make.' Thomas nodded slowly. He bought one sharpener, skipped the paper sweets, and kept twelve tokens 'for next month's shop day.' Later I heard him tell Rafiq, 'You're good at prices.' Next step: I will let Thomas and Rafiq plan the prices together for the next shop day, and ask the whole class to find out what a few things cost at home.

qa.q: How many tokens did each child have?
qa.a: Each child had twenty tokens.

qa.q: What does Thomas's comment to Rafiq suggest he felt?
qa.a: He seemed to admire how Rafiq understood why things cost what they did.

qa.q: Why is the teacher's next step a good way to support this?
qa.a: Planning prices lets the boys practise judging what things are worth, and asking about home links tokens to real money.

qa.q: How might Rafiq have felt when Thomas praised his prices?
qa.a: He likely felt proud and noticed, since his explanation had been taken seriously. 😊

grounding: Illustrates a child treating tokens as value to compare and save rather than spend on everything at once.

passage: Dear diary, today Jasleen got a new sparkly pencil box AGAIN. Her old one is fine, only the zip is stuck. I wanted to cry a bit because mine is the one Didi used. At home I counted my tin. Ninety-two rupees. The box costs one hundred and fifty. Mummy said if I want, I can put in ten rupees every Sunday and it will take six Sundays. Six!! Then I tried the candle trick on my old zip, like Nanaji showed me, and it slides now. So maybe I will save for the storybook instead. Don't know yet. Also Jasleen threw away a notebook with half the pages empty. I took it. Rough work for a month, free. – Indu

qa.q: How much money was in Indu's tin?
qa.a: Ninety-two rupees.

qa.q: Why did Indu feel like crying at first?
qa.a: Indu wanted a shiny new box like Jasleen's, but Indu's own box was a hand-me-down from Didi.

qa.q: What could Mummy do to keep supporting Indu's saving?
qa.a: Mummy could help Indu keep track of the Sunday savings so Indu sees the goal get closer, and let Indu choose between the box and the book.

qa.q: How might Jasleen see the notebook Indu took?
qa.a: Jasleen probably saw it as used and not worth keeping, while Indu saw a month of free rough paper.

grounding: Shows a child counting savings toward a goal, repairing instead of replacing, and reusing what others waste.

passage: At the temple fair in the small town, Pranav, ten, had fifty rupees from his Nani. The plastic gun at Bhupen's stall cost forty. "It breaks in a week," said his cousin. Pranav picked it up, put it down, picked it up again. Then he walked past the stalls, comparing. A kite and a big spool of string cost thirty together. He bought them and kept twenty in his pocket. Bhupen laughed. "Thinking like a shopkeeper." That evening the kite flew higher than the neighbour's.

qa.q: How much did the plastic gun cost?
qa.a: Forty rupees.

qa.q: What was Pranav feeling as he picked the gun up and put it down?
qa.a: He felt tempted but unsure whether it was worth the money.

qa.q: What would you advise Pranav about the twenty rupees left over?
qa.a: Talk with Nani or a parent about whether to save it or spend it on something he really values.

qa.q: How might Bhupen see Pranav's choice?
qa.a: With amused respect, seeing a boy who compared prices carefully.

grounding: Shows a child comparing value at a fair and choosing something longer-lasting over a quick buy.

passage: In their small flat in Taipei, Mei, eleven, caught her younger brother Wei leaving the bathroom light on again. "Electricity costs money," she said, flicking it off. She had been saving her pocket money in a jar for three months for a book on birds. When her schoolbag strap broke, her mother offered a new one. Mei shook her head, found a needle and thread, and stitched it. "It works," she told Wei. "Then the money can go to the book." Wei watched her, then turned off his own lamp.

qa.q: What was Mei saving for?
qa.a: A book on birds.

qa.q: Why did Mei choose to stitch her bag instead of getting a new one?
qa.a: She felt determined and a little proud, wanting to save her money for the book she really wanted.

qa.q: What might help Mei decide when to repair and when to replace?
qa.a: Asking her mother whether the repair is safe and will last, so she can make a sensible choice.

qa.q: How might Wei see his older sister's choices?
qa.a: He seems to admire her a little, since he starts copying her by turning off his lamp.

grounding: Shows a child valuing money and resources by saving, repairing and not wasting electricity.

passage: In the school canteen, Gurleen, twelve, watched half-eaten plates of rice go into the big bin. Wasim, the canteen uncle, sighed. "Every day, a full bin." Gurleen thought of the dal her mother measured each morning. She made a sign: "Take what you'll eat. Come back for more." She stuck it above the serving counter with Wasim's permission. The first week, the bin was only half full. Wasim gave her a thumbs up. "Saved one whole pot today."

qa.q: What did Gurleen's sign say?
qa.a: "Take what you'll eat. Come back for more."

qa.q: What was Gurleen feeling when she watched the rice go into the bin?
qa.a: She was bothered and uneasy about the waste, thinking of how carefully her mother measured food.

qa.q: What made Gurleen's plan work?
qa.a: It was simple, she asked Wasim first, and it let students take more if they needed it.

qa.q: How might Wasim feel about the change?
qa.a: Relieved and appreciative that less food and effort were being wasted.

grounding: Shows a child noticing wasted resources in her school canteen and acting to reduce it.

passage: I'm Charu. I live next door to Noor's family. Last Sunday I saw Noor, who's ten, standing at the toy stall outside the market with her birthday money in her hand, looking at a flashing plastic sword. She picked it up, pressed the button, put it down. Picked it up again. Then she put it down and bought a set of coloured pencils instead, from the stationery shop. I don't know why. At home she went round switching off the fans in rooms no one was in. Her grandmother watched and smiled. Maybe she'd been taught something at school.

qa.q: What did Noor buy instead of the sword?
qa.a: A set of coloured pencils.

qa.q: What might Noor have been feeling as she kept picking up the sword and putting it down?
qa.a: She was probably torn between the fun of the sword and whether it was worth her birthday money.

qa.q: How could Noor's grandmother support her thinking?
qa.a: She could ask Noor what made her choose the pencils and talk about what makes something good value.

qa.q: How does Charu see Noor's choices?
qa.a: Charu is curious and a bit impressed, but can only guess at her reasons.

grounding: A neighbour watches a ten-year-old choose useful pencils over a flashy toy and switch off unused fans.

passage:
Week one: Usha saw a pencil box with a magnet lid in the shop. She asked her mother, who said, "Let's think about it." Usha pouted all evening.
Week three: Usha had been putting her small birthday coins in a jar. She counted them with her friend Bidisha. Not enough. Bidisha said, "My old box still works. Why do you need a new one?" Usha paused.
Week five: Usha went to the shop with her mother and the jar. She looked at the magnet box, then at a cheaper one that did the same job. She chose the cheaper one. "Now I'll still have some coins left," she said, and felt oddly proud.

qa.q: What was special about the pencil box Usha first wanted?
qa.a: It had a magnet lid.

qa.q: How did Usha feel when she chose the cheaper box?
qa.a: She felt oddly proud of her choice and happy to have some coins left.

qa.q: What choice did Usha make, and what helped her think it through?
qa.a: She chose the cheaper box that did the same job, after saving for a while and hearing Bidisha's question.

qa.q: How might Usha's mother see her daughter's choice?
qa.a: She would likely feel proud and pleased at how carefully Usha chose. 😊

grounding: Over five weeks, a girl moves from wanting a fancy pencil box to choosing a cheaper one that does the same job.

passage: Anand Dadu pointed at Eshaan's pile of half-used notebooks. "When I was nine, beta, I got one notebook for the whole term. One. I wrote in pencil, small, on both sides, and when it was full I rubbed out the first pages and used them again. I remember wanting a new one badly. But I knew my father worked all month for what we had. One day I found a rich boy's thrown-away notebook, half empty, in the gutter. I dried it in the sun and it lasted me another month." Eshaan looked at his pile. "So I should use these first?" Dadu smiled. "What do you think?"

qa.q: How many notebooks did young Anand get for the whole term?
qa.a: One.

qa.q: How did young Anand feel when he found the half-empty notebook?
qa.a: He likely felt lucky and thankful, having wanted a new notebook badly.

qa.q: What was the choice young Anand made in the story, and why?
qa.a: He dried and used a thrown-away notebook instead of wishing for a new one, because he respected how hard his father worked.

qa.q: How might Eshaan's view of his own notebooks change after the story?
qa.a: Eshaan may start to see the half-used notebooks as worth finishing before asking for new ones.

grounding: A grandfather tells his grandson how he made one notebook last and reused a discarded one as a child.

passage:
At the temple fair, Dhruv, ten, had a hundred rupees of birthday money and only half an hour before Papa came back.

He saw a plastic toy car for eighty. "I want that!"

His sister Ritu pulled his arm. "Look around first."

At the next stall, a wooden spinning top was thirty. At another, the same car was fifty.

Dhruv stood there, thinking. The first car broke easily; he'd had one before. He bought the top for thirty and kept seventy in his pocket.

"What will you do with the rest?" Ritu asked.

"Save it. For the cricket bat."

qa.q: How much did the wooden spinning top cost?
qa.a: The wooden spinning top was thirty.

qa.q: How did Dhruv feel when he first saw the plastic car?
qa.a: Dhruv felt excited and eager, wanting it straight away.

qa.q: What helped Dhruv make a thoughtful choice?
qa.a: Ritu's advice to look around first and remembering that the car broke easily helped.

qa.q: How might Ritu feel when Dhruv decided to save?
qa.a: Ritu likely felt proud of her brother's choice.

grounding: With little time and money at a fair, a boy compares prices, avoids wasteful spending and saves for a goal.

passage:
In the Diwali week in Jaipur, every shop in the colony sold crackers. Vaibhav bought a big box. Ramesh, eleven, had his own savings in a tin.

"Buy some, na!" Vaibhav said.

Ramesh looked at the prices. The box would cost almost everything in his tin. He was saving for a cricket bat.

"I'll share yours," he said, grinning.

That evening, he also noticed all the fairy lights left on in the day. He switched them off and told his mother. "The electricity bill," he said, the way his father did.

His mother laughed. "Who taught you that?"

qa.q: What was Ramesh saving for?
qa.a: He was saving for a cricket bat.

qa.q: How did Ramesh feel when Vaibhav urged him to buy crackers?
qa.a: Ramesh was tempted but determined to keep his savings for the bat.

qa.q: How did Ramesh show respect for resource limits?
qa.a: He saved his money and switched off fairy lights left on in the day.

qa.q: How might Ramesh's mother feel when he mentioned the electricity bill?
qa.a: His mother was amused and probably proud.

grounding: During Diwali, a boy avoids spending his savings on crackers and switches off wasted lights.

passage:
"Abhinav, the tap!" Pallavi shouted. It was May, and the tank on their Nagpur building was already half empty.

"I'm just washing my hands."

"For five minutes? Water's short this summer. Close it while you soap."

Abhinav turned it off. "Fine. But you left half your dal at lunch."

Pallavi opened her mouth, then shut it. "Okay. That's fair."

"So tomorrow you take less, and I use less water."

"And we tell Papa to fix the dripping tap in the bathroom."

"Deal."

qa.q: Why was water short?
qa.a: It was May, and the building tank was already half empty.

qa.q: How did Pallavi feel when Abhinav mentioned her dal?
qa.a: Pallavi felt caught out and a bit embarrassed, then admitted it was fair.

qa.q: What did Pallavi and Abhinav agree to do?
qa.a: Take less food, use less water, and ask Papa to fix the dripping tap.

qa.q: How might Papa feel hearing their plan?
qa.a: Papa would likely feel pleased that they're caring about resources.

grounding: In a water-short summer, a brother and sister agree to avoid wasting water and food.

passage: Last Eid I got three hundred rupees as Eidi from my uncles and aunts. I'm Zainab, and I spent it all in one afternoon at the mall: glitter pens, a squishy toy and two cold coffees. By evening the squishy toy had split. My brother Sahil had kept his Eidi in a tin. This Ramzan he bought the football he'd wanted for months, and Abbu said, "See, he knew what it was worth." I felt silly and a bit jealous. This Eid I kept my money in an envelope for two weeks before deciding. I bought a proper sketchbook. It's still in one piece.

qa.q: How much Eidi did Zainab get last Eid?
qa.a: Three hundred rupees.

qa.q: How did Zainab feel when Abbu praised Sahil?
qa.a: Zainab felt silly and a bit jealous, seeing how Sahil's waiting had paid off.

qa.q: What choice helped Zainab this Eid?
qa.a: Keeping the money in an envelope for two weeks gave Zainab time to choose something lasting; talking choices over with Abbu could help too.

qa.q: How might Sahil feel about finally buying the football?
qa.a: Sahil probably feels proud and satisfied after waiting months for something he really wanted.

grounding: Illustrates a child learning, over two Eids, to weigh what money is worth before spending it.
